QF.id: AIFM Modern Portfolio Theory and Capital Market Theory_10

question.text: Ms. Anjali Nair, CIO of Brahmaputra Alternatives AIF, observes that when she plugs her Venture Capital fund's NAV-based quarterly returns into a Markowitz optimiser alongside listed equity, the optimiser recommends an aggressively high weight to VC. What is the MOST likely cause of this misleading output?

answer.text: Private-market returns reported on a lagged/smoothed basis artificially depress estimated variance and correlation with listed equities, leading the optimiser to overstate the diversification benefit of the AIF.
The Markowitz model is mathematically invalid for illiquid assets and cannot be used at all.
The SEBI AIF Regulations prohibit the use of MPT for Category I and II AIFs, requiring a factor-based approach instead.
Since the J-curve always produces positive early returns, the optimiser simply chases that alpha.

explanation.text: The Logic: This is the classic illiquid-asset 'stale NAV' problem. Quarterly, appraisal-based NAVs smooth the true volatility and dampen estimated correlation with public markets. Input variance is understated, covariance is understated, and the mean-variance optimiser responds by over-allocating to the AIF. This is a well-known 'estimation risk' issue flagged in Chapter 4.11. The Trap: B is too strong — MPT is used, just with cleansed inputs. C fabricates a regulation. D is backwards — the J-curve produces NEGATIVE returns early. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B and XV address smoothing and stale prices. XIX-B (Cat III distributor) touches liquidity-smoothing in the context of hedge-fund-style AIFs. Manager's Pro-Tip: Always de-smooth AIF returns (Geltner or Getmansky-Lo-Makarov unsmoothing) before feeding them into a SAA model. Disclose the de-smoothing in the PPM's Risk Factors section — LP due-diligence teams will ask.
